Besides the obvious variables of title, genre, director, year, and duration, the rest of the variables are as follows:

  • gross : The gross earnings in the US box office, not adjusted for inflation
  • budget: The movie's budget
  • cast_facebook_likes: the number of facebook likes cast memebrs received
  • votes: the number of people who voted for (or rated) the movie in IMDB
  • reviews: the number of reviews for that movie
  • rating: IMDB average rating

Produce a table with the average gross earning and budget (gross and budget) by genre. Calculate a variable return_on_budget which shows how many $ did a movie make at the box office for each $ of its budget. Ranked genres by this return_on_budget in descending order

    .groupby('genre')\
    .agg({

In [90]:
number_of_buckets = 5
bucket_labels = [f'Bucket {number}' for number in range(1, number_of_buckets + 1)]

# Rank first so repeated review counts do not create very uneven buckets.
movies['reviews_bucket'] = pd.qcut(
    movies['reviews'].rank(method='first'),
    q=number_of_buckets,
    labels=bucket_labels
)

ratings_by_reviews = (
    movies.groupby('reviews_bucket', observed=False)
    .agg(
        minimum_reviews=('reviews', 'min'),
        maximum_reviews=('reviews', 'max'),
        mean_gross=('gross', 'mean'),
        minimum_gross=('gross', 'min'),
        maximum_gross=('gross', 'max'),
        median_gross=('gross', 'median'),
        standard_deviation_gross=('gross', 'std'),
        movie_count=('reviews', 'size')
    )
    .reset_index()
)

ratings_by_reviews['review_range'] = (
    ratings_by_reviews['minimum_reviews'].astype(int).astype(str)
    + ' - '
    + ratings_by_reviews['maximum_reviews'].astype(int).astype(str)
)

ratings_by_reviews = ratings_by_reviews[
    [
        'reviews_bucket',
        'review_range',
        'movie_count',
        'mean_gross',
        'minimum_gross',
        'maximum_gross',
        'median_gross',
        'standard_deviation_gross'
    ]
].sort_values('mean_gross', ascending=False)

ratings_by_reviews.columns = [
    'Reviews bucket',
    'Review range',
    'Movie count',
    'Mean gross',
    'Minimum gross',
    'Maximum gross',
    'Median gross',
    'Standard Deviation gross'
]

ratings_by_reviews['Mean gross'] = ratings_by_reviews['Mean gross'].round(4)
ratings_by_reviews['Standard Deviation gross'] = ratings_by_reviews['Standard Deviation gross'].round(4)
display(ratings_by_reviews)

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
sns.boxplot(
    data=movies,
    x='gross',
    hue='reviews_bucket'
)
plt.title('Distribution of Gross Revenues by Review Bucket')
plt.xscale('log')
plt.xlabel('Gross Revenue')
plt.ylabel('Review Bucket')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Conclusion¶

The results suggest that movies in buckets with a higher number of reviews (like bucket 5)tend to have higher average gross revenue. However, the distribution for all the buckets seems to be wide (x axis in log scale because its a very large value)

Produce a scatterplot and write one sentence discussing whether the number of facebook likes that the cast has received is likely to be a good predictor of how much money a movie will make at the box office. What variable are you going to map to the Y- and X- axes?

sns.scatterplot(
    data=movies,
    x='cast_facebook_likes',
    y='gross')

This scatterplot using logaritmic scales on both axis chart allows to see that there is a weak positive trend relationship between the number of likes of the cast on facebook and the gross revenues. If I where to explore this feature to a model, I would probably avoid it, datapoints show a very wide variance.

Examine the relationship between gross and budget. Produce a scatterplot and write one sentence discussing whether budget is likely to be a good predictor of how much money a movie will make at the box office.

In [92]:
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
sns.scatterplot(
    data=movies,
    x='gross',
    y='budget',
    )
plt.xscale('log')
plt.yscale('log')
plt.title('Relationship Between Gross Revenue and Budget')
plt.xlabel('Gross Revenues')
plt.ylabel('Budget')
Out[92]:
Text(0, 0.5, 'Budget')

It is possible to visualize a positive correlation between budget and gross revenues. Low budget movies are prone to have more variance in its revenues, while high budget movies seem to have a positive monotonic increment on the revenue showing less variance.

Examine the relationship between gross and rating. Produce a scatterplot, faceted by genre and discuss whether IMDB ratings are likely to be a good predictor of how much money a movie will make at the box office. Is there anything strange in this dataset?

In [93]:
(
    sns.relplot(
        data=movies,
        x='rating',
        y='gross',
        col='genre',
        col_wrap=3,
        height=4,
        aspect=1.2,
        hue='genre',
        facet_kws={'sharex': False, 'sharey': True}
    )
    .set_titles(col_template='Genre: {col_name}', size=11, weight='bold')
    .set_axis_labels('Rating', 'Gross Revenues (Log)')
    .set(yscale='log')
    .fig.suptitle('Relationship Between Gross Revenue and Rating by Genre', fontsize=16, y=1.03)
)

plt.show()

There are some genres in which there are not enough data to conclude like:

  • Thriller
  • western
  • romance
  • sci-fi
  • Fantasy
  • Documentary
  • Musical

And there is also some generes for which the positive relationship is also not as strong as the others (its worth to check if this is due to the sample size):

  • Horror
  • Animation
  • Biography
  • Adventure

movie_list = ['Adventure', 'Action', 'Biography', 'Comedy', 'Horror', 'Crime', 'Drama']



plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))

sns.boxplot(
    data=movies.query('genre.isin(@movie_list)'),
    x='gross',
    hue='genre'
)
plt.title('Distribution of Gross Revenues by Movie Genre')
plt.xscale('log')
plt.xlabel('Gross Revenue')
plt.ylabel('Genre')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Conclusion¶

The boxplot suggests that Action and Adventure movies generally achieve higher gross revenues than the other selected genres, with higher central values and broader upper ranges(mean and median). However the distributions also overlap considerably, meaning that genre alone does not guarantee high revenue
